items.question: How do you see the relationship between generative AI models' power and the challenges they pose for responsible AI?
items.object: Generative AI models' open-endedness and responsible AI
items.answer: I think the top-level summary is that the power of these models is in their open-endedness. They're not making numerical predictions about inputs or point predictions or solving classification problems. They are truly generative, and that very open-endedness that is the power of these models is also a source of the challenges for responsible AI.
quotes: I think the top-level summary is that the power of these models is in their open-endedness. They're not making numerical predictions about inputs or point predictions or solving classification problems. They are truly generative, and that very open-endedness that is the power of these models is also a source of the challenges for responsible AI.

rubrics.text: The response identifies open-endedness as the source of generative AI models' power.
The response identifies generative AI models' open-endedness as a source of responsible AI challenges.

items.question: How do you assess the progress of Amazon’s AI service cards over the past year?
items.object: Amazon AI service cards and their development process
items.answer: So that process that was new and announced just a year ago at re:Invent is now a well-oiled machine. Still a lot of work to do, but we're getting more of the cards out, and I think the cards are becoming more informative, more sophisticated. As I think I probably mentioned a year ago, those cards are really meant to be general audience summaries of the properties of our models and services and recommended use cases, and some performance metrics and responsible AI metrics. With a year-plus under our belt of developing these things, we're really getting it down.

items.question: How do you see generative AI changing the challenges of developing AI service cards?
items.object: Developing AI service cards in the generative AI era
items.answer: I think part of what we've learned is that there will be new challenges in developing these cards in the generative AI era. When we talked a year ago, I think we were largely talking about models that took as input something like a consumer loan application and output a prediction of whether somebody will repay or not. There's no notion of hallucination in the output of such a model. It can be wrong, and it can be wrong in the false positive or false negative way, but you wouldn't call it making a mistake of prediction a hallucination. A lot of the challenges that we and the industry have faced in the last year is adapting our way of thinking about responsible AI to incorporate these new considerations like toxicity, hallucination, in many cases intellectual property concerns and the like.
quotes: I think part of what we've learned is that there will be new challenges in developing these cards in the generative AI era.

items.question: How do you approach deciding what to report in responsible AI cards for generative AI models?
items.object: Reporting responsible AI metrics for generative AI
items.answer: The stuff that gets into the cards, for the most part, is either qualitative guidance, primarily intended for customers but meant for anybody who's interested, as well as more quantitative metrics around both outright performance as well as responsible AI metrics. When it comes to metrics, we report on the things that we feel like we can sensibly report on. There's a lot of things in the generative space that the industry and even the underlying science has not yet come to good ways of measuring. For instance, if a writer feels that a large language model is appropriating their style, I will be the first to admit we don't have good quantitative ways of measuring that or talking about it or mitigating it yet. This is a lot of the science work that we're doing internally at AWS, but that's also going on in the external research community as well.

items.question: What do you see as the central challenge in developing benchmarks and metrics for large language models?
items.object: Coverage in benchmarks and metrics for large language models
items.answer: I think the problem with these things is that it's not just the open-endedness of the output that matters, it's the open-endedness of the input. If you compare the before times, pre-generative era, something like face recognition, where the input is an image and it's only relevant if there's a face in it, first of all, and then secondly the output is very constrained. It's like, is this an image of somebody in this database, or are these two images the face of the same person? A lot of the challenges in developing these benchmarks and metrics is just getting coverage.

items.question: How do you think about coverage when evaluating machine learning models?
items.object: Coverage in evaluating machine learning models
items.answer: Both in the input and output sense. For instance, if I'm doing face recognition or some other computer vision task like object classification in an image, I want my inputs to explore the natural variation in facial images in terms of lighting and angle of pose and occlusions. It's already quite challenging to get that variation in such a constrained problem, where the input is an image with a face in it and you want to make some prediction about whether it's a person in your database.

items.question: What do you see as the main challenges in evaluating large language models?
items.object: Coverage and metric selection in large language model evaluation
items.answer: When the input is any sentence that anybody could imagine entering into an LLM and the output is a free-form continuation of the prompt, it's just very difficult to get very good coverage of all the natural use cases that might arise. I think we are starting down this road, and this offering is a great start. What ends up being challenging is you end up looking at this table in which the rows are many different LLMs and the columns are dozens of different metrics, and then you're suddenly swimming in a sea of numbers. It's kind of like even in traditional notions of fairness in machine learning: there's too many reasonable definitions. It's like the old cliche, the great thing about standards is that there's so many to choose from. Ideally, over time we'll figure out what are the metrics for which we can get good coverage and which are the right independent ones. You don't want too many metrics that are measuring the same thing, because then you're drowning in a sea of numbers.

items.question: How do you think the standard for hallucination should vary across uses of an LLM for writing?
items.object: Hallucination standards for LLM-assisted writing
items.answer: So let's just take writing, right? If I'm using an LLM for helping write journalism, there's a very strong standard of hallucination there. If I'm using it to write historical fiction, well, it's fiction, but it's historical fiction, and so you want some alignment with the actual facts. There your tolerance for hallucination might be higher because there's the fiction part of it, but you're not going to just allow anything because it's historical fiction, versus true fiction where you might arguably say it's not possible for an LLM to hallucinate if it is actually being used to generate or be an aid in the creation of fiction.

items.question: Why do you see use-case-specific metrics as important for evaluating responsible generative AI?
items.object: Use-case-specific metrics for responsible generative AI
items.answer: Same thing with toxicity. If I'm using an LLM as a creative tool for writing children's books, my tolerance for any kind of offensive, disturbing language is going to be zero. For a different use case I might have a higher tolerance for it. I do think that the greatest leverage that we'll eventually get towards the open-endedness challenges that generative AI presents to responsible AI and even just to measuring performance will come from settling on more specific use cases and developing metrics for those specific use cases as well.

items.question: How do you understand the tradeoff between a foundation model’s generality and its performance on a specific use case?
items.object: The tradeoff between foundation-model generality and use-case specificity
items.answer: There's always a cost for generality. If I, as a mathematician or a theoretician, look at some theorem and it's a very general statement, when I look at that I say there's going to be a price to be paid for that, because you're covering a lot of cases. What you can say about a broader set of circumstances is going to be necessarily weaker than you could say about a narrower set of circumstances. We're seeing that tension between the better performance you can get by specificity of use case versus the generality of the underlying foundation model. That tension is something that's very actively being played out both in industry and in the science as well.

items.question: How do you think interventions that steer LLMs toward trusted information and away from toxicity should evolve?

items.answer: I predict that over time we will and should figure out ways of taking these post hoc interventions on the natural myopic way that LLMs behave and figure out how to endogenize it, how to embed those desiderata, like accessing external information resources that are trusted and verifiable or suppressing toxicity. We need to figure out ways of getting those into the model training process itself, so that you don't have all these little pieces of software watching what the model is doing and stepping in and saying, no, no, no, don't do that.

items.question: How do you think large language models have changed in the way they assign pronouns when gender is ambiguous?
items.object: Gender assumptions and pronoun balancing in large language models
items.answer: I remember, before the release of ChatGPT but not too much more, I was playing around with a bunch of LLMs that were accessible within the science community. Anytime you typed in an ungendered name like Chris or Pat, and then the continuation would assign pronouns to it, it would generally assign male pronouns to ungendered names. If you typed in something like Dr. Hansen it would choose male pronouns; if you said Nurse Hansen it would choose female pronouns. As far as I can tell—I haven't done an actual scientific study—the LLMs that are out there are much, much better at balancing the distribution of pronouns in cases where it might be ambiguous.

items.question: How do you distinguish guardrail models from RLHF when it comes to controlling an LLM's responses about demographic characteristics?
items.object: Guardrail models versus RLHF for controlling LLM responses
items.answer: The kind of intervention that I just mentioned would be a guardrail model, because it's actually stepping in and saying, “Sorry, this interaction is not going to happen.” RLHF would, I think, give you output, but would it sanitize it more? Of course, depending on what the humans in the RLHF did, because they're the ones providing the guidance to the training process. items.question: How do you understand the way AWS's differential privacy offering answers aggregate queries about a private data set?
items.object: AWS's differential privacy offering
items.answer: At a high level, the way it works is I have a proprietary private data set over here, and you and I have a mutual interest in letting you make aggregated queries to that data set, like what is the percentage of users in the database that live in the greater Seattle area, are interested in video games, and are between the ages of 19 and 35? There's some numerical answer to that. In the differential privacy offering, rather than just computing the answer to numerical precision and then giving it to you, I compute it to numerical precision and then add a bit of noise. I do add some randomization to the answer. If the actual answer was 16.9%, I might return an answer to you that's anywhere between 16.5 and 18.4, something like this.

items.question: How do you understand the tradeoff involved in adding noise to query answers for differential privacy?
items.object: Adding noise to query answers for differential privacy
items.answer: The addition of the noise to the answer to the query, in a mathematically provable sense, gives me some security guarantee about your ability to reverse engineer information about specific individuals in the data set. But it still allows me to give you, in a very provably private way, aggregate information about the data set that doesn't let you exfiltrate information about individuals. Not surprisingly, the more noise I add to this number, the greater the privacy guarantee, but of course the less accuracy the answer will have.

items.question: How do you explain differentially private synthetic data generation as an alternative to answering aggregate questions about private data?
items.object: Differentially private synthetic data generation
items.answer: The idea is that, just take the same scenario: I've got this private data set and I'm going to let you ask a series of aggregate questions. I'm going to add noise to their answers in a way that provides privacy guarantees. An alternate model is, well, I'm just going to give you a data set. It's not going to be the private data set, of course, but it'll be a data set that I've added noise to. It's easy to imagine adding noise to a number. What does it mean to add noise to a data set? That's probably a little bit beyond our scope, but there are basically well-understood ways of starting with a private data set, producing a randomized version of that data set that has provable privacy guarantees and preserves a great deal of the statistical structure of the original data set.

items.question: What do you see as the scientific holy grail for differentially private synthetic data?
items.object: Differentially private synthetic data that supports arbitrary downstream machine learning
items.answer: Instead of us engaging in this sequence of you ask me a question, I give you a noisy answer, you ask me another question, I give you a noisy answer ad infinitum, I just say, “Sam, here's a version of the data set. Ask any question that you want of it.” The scientific holy grail of this, which is an unsolved scientific problem, which is why it's a holy grail, is that I basically give you a private version of my data set, a differentially private version of my data set, that supports arbitrary downstream machine learning. Rather than just answering simple aggregate questions of the type that I mentioned, the goal would be, “Sam, here's the differentially private version of the data set. Any ML experiment you run on this data set—you decide which column you want to predict from the other columns, you pick your model architecture, you pick your hyperparameters—I give you some kind of guarantee that no matter what you do on the synthetic data set I gave you, you will get similar results to what you would have gotten on the original data set.” This is an exciting open science problem that we and others are working hard on.

items.question: How do you understand the importance of data modality in responsible AI fairness work?
items.object: Data modality and the assumptions of fairness research
items.answer: One of our learnings is just how much modality matters. A lot of the literature on fairness in the research community more or less starts from the conceptual point that you have a tabular data set in which the demographic properties of the individuals that you might want to protect against harm are already in the data set. There's a column for race and a column for age and a column for gender, and the science problem is, knowing those demographic attributes, how do you make sure that no particular subgroup is being harmed compared to the general population in the data set?
quotes: As an example, one of those learnings is just how much modality matters.

items.question: How do you think fairness should be approached in speech recognition when the audio data lacks demographic annotations?
items.object: Fairness in speech recognition
items.answer: In speech recognition, for example, the data is not annotated for that. You get an audio frequency signal of my spoken speech, and you might try to infer my gender, but in general the correlations between things like race and what you can detect in an acoustic signal of speech are very weak. On the other hand, what you can detect are things like regional accent and dialects, like the vocabulary I choose to use, and also my accent. I think the sensible thing to do there is not to try to project or impute these traditional demographic categories onto that data, but rather to take the data as it comes to you and enforce responsible AI and fairness considerations with what you can measure, which is the thing that actually naturally varies in the data set.

items.question: How do you think AI activism should fit into developers’ efforts to enforce responsible AI principles?
items.object: AI activism and bias bounties
items.answer: At AWS, no matter how hard we try, we cannot anticipate and test for every possible downstream use case by customers. It's just not feasible. It's not just about anticipating the use cases of your customers; it's anticipating what journalists, nonprofits, researchers might do in a less-than-friendly audit of your model. We think that AI activism movement is a healthy force in the industry right now. This notion of bias bounties that's been in the air for a couple of years is inviting the external community into the process of enforcing responsible AI principles in a more cooperative way rather than a more adversarial one, where you have a model out with an API and a combination of a journalist and a scientist go and perform some audit on it without your knowledge or approval, and then the first time the developer reads about it is when it's in the news and it's blowing up, and then you have to react to it. There are technical ideas in the air about how to do that integration of the activist community into a more cooperative relationship with developers.

items.question: How do you feel about the public attention and hype that ChatGPT has brought to machine learning?
items.object: The public attention and hype surrounding ChatGPT
items.answer: I'm only half-joking when I say, I have the benefit of being in the machine learning area—I know that it's only been an industry for about a decade, but I've been a researcher in it since the '80s, so we're pushing on 40 years now. I never thought I would, for so many decades, have my non-work friends be suitably impressed with what I did but not want to know too much about it. I have to admit, I'm dying to go out to a dinner where the topic of conversation isn't ChatGPT and people asking me about ChatGPT. I would welcome a little bit of attenuation of the hype, but in general I think it's been a great thing for the industry and a very exciting time scientifically as well.
